query: For reported HfNbTiVAl10 with a hierarchical heterostructure, what testable hypothesis could enable Young’s modulus, yield strength, and fracture-related behavior to be predicted more rapidly and accurately under tensile and fracture testing than with established simulations? State the hypothesized rationale, the measurable gains in predictive accuracy and efficiency, circumstances in which the hypothesis may fail, relevant supporting evidence, and a predeclared result from independent measurements that would decisively falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: A hybrid physics‐informed machine learning model that is explicitly trained on hierarchical heterostructure descriptors (e.g., phase fractions, interfacial features and nano‐precipitate distributions) and key ab initio parameters (e.g., elastic constants, misfit volumes, and stacking fault energies) can rapidly predict Young’s modulus, yield strength, and fracture behavior of HfNbTiVAl10 under tensile and fracture loading with significantly reduced computational cost and improved predictive accuracy compared to conventional full-scale simulations. It achieves this by learning the interplay of microstructural mediators that govern deformation mechanisms.
generation.material_initial_state: HfNbTiVAl10 in its as‐processed state exhibiting a hierarchical heterostructure with multiple length scales (e.g., nanoscale precipitates embedded within a matrix and chemically distinct interfacial regions).
generation.intervention: Develop and deploy a machine learning–based predictive framework that integrates physics-based features (derived from ab initio and calibrated experimental data) with structural descriptors quantifying the hierarchical heterostructure.
generation.conditions: Tensile and quasi‐static/fracture testing performed at room temperature (and optionally at higher temperatures) with well‐characterized sample microstructures; the ML framework is trained on datasets that include both simulation outputs and experimental measurements under similar processing conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: Descriptors of the hierarchical microstructure such as nano-precipitate size, spatial distribution, phase volume fractions, and interfacial chemical composition are encoded as features in the model to mediate the microstructure–property relationships.
generation.mechanism: By incorporating both traditional physics-based parameters (e.g., computed elastic constants, stacking fault energies) and explicit descriptors of the heterostructure, the model can ‘learn’ the dominant deformation mechanisms (such as dislocation glide/blocking at interfaces and strain partitioning between phases) that govern the elastic, yield, and fracture responses, reducing reliance on computationally intensive simulations while exploiting established physical insights.
generation.predicted_outcome: The proposed framework is expected to reduce prediction time by an order of magnitude relative to full-scale ab initio or molecular dynamics simulations and improve the prediction accuracy (with errors reduced to within approximately 5–10% of experimental values) for Young’s modulus, yield strength, and fracture-related behaviors.
generation.baseline: Current established simulation methods (e.g., full ab initio calculations, MD simulations) which are computationally intensive and can exhibit larger discrepancies when extrapolated to complex hierarchical microstructures.
generation.boundary: The approach may fail if the actual microstructural complexity (e.g., unexpected phase transformations, severe defects, or non-representative heterogeneity) falls outside the domain of the training data, or if significant measurement uncertainties mask the microstructure–property correlations.
generation.uncertainty: While improvements in computational efficiency and predictive accuracy are anticipated based on similar successes in HEA property prediction, the exact magnitude of gains (i.e., the precise error reduction and speedup factors) depends on the quality and representativeness of the training dataset and the fidelity of the microstructural descriptors.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a series of HfNbTiVAl10 samples with systematically varied hierarchical microstructures. Use both conventional full-scale simulations and the new ML framework to predict Young’s modulus, yield strength, and fracture behavior under identical tensile and fracture testing conditions. Compare the predictions from the ML model with independently measured experimental data.
measurements: Young’s modulus determined via dynamic or quasi-static tensile tests
Yield strength from standard 0.2% offset criteria in tensile tests
Fracture behavior metrics such as crack initiation load and crack propagation patterns from fracture tests
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the ML framework’s predictions fail to achieve a prediction error below ~10% (or do not show a speedup of at least one order of magnitude) relative to conventional simulations, or if the predicted trends in properties with changes in hierarchical features are not observed experimentally, then the hypothesis is decisively falsified.

cited_evidence.text: A typical method of choice for truly predictive calculations of alloy properties is density functional theory (DFT). However, explicit evaluation of fracture or yield strength in alloys is mostly out of reach for available DFT implementations. Although this may become possible with general-purpose interatomic potentials,, a fairly robust description can be obtained by using appropriate models, which have been shown to accurately predict strengthening and ductility. These models combine linear elasticity and microscopic principles, and the only required input parameters are certain material properties. Specifically, apart from basic equilibrium properties, such as the molar volume and elastic constants, the strengthening model requires misfit volumes related to concentration derivatives of the alloy volume, while the ductility model relies on surface and unstable stacking fault (USF) energies computed for specific orientations. Importantly, all of these parameters are accessible through simulations using first-principles methods, yet, such simulations are still challenging for disordered MPEAs.

Our use of a Genetic Algorithm (GA) for feature selection enhances the model’s performance by systematically evaluating and selecting the most relevant features. This approach improves predictive accuracy and provides insights into the physical significance of each feature, further validating our model’s interpretability. This interpretability is crucial for understanding the underlying mechanisms governing the mechanical properties of HEAs. The insights gained from our models can guide the design of new high-performance HEAs. By understanding the role of key features and their interactions, researchers can tailor alloy compositions to achieve desired mechanical properties, thus accelerating the discovery and optimization of advanced materials. Future work could explore the integration of additional physics-based features and the application of more advanced ensemble learning techniques. Expanding the dataset to include more diverse alloy compositions and testing conditions could further enhance the model’s robustness and applicability.

AbstractA hierarchical microstructure strengthened high entropy superalloy (HESA) with superior cost specific yield strength from room temperature up to 1,023 K is presented. By phase transformation pathway through metastability, HESA possesses a hierarchical microstructure containing a dispersion of nano size disordered FCC particles inside ordered L12 precipitates that are within the FCC matrix. The average tensile yield strength of HESA from room temperature to 1,023 K could be 120 MPa higher than that of advanced single crystal superalloy, while HESA could still exhibit an elongation greater than 20%. Furthermore, the cost specific yield strength of HESA can be 8 times that of some superalloys. A template for lighter, stronger, cheaper, and more ductile high temperature alloy is proposed.Subject terms: Mechanical properties, Metals and alloys
